title: Israel among the empires

scope.to: Judean communities in the sixth and fifth centuries BCE
scope.focus: Israel and Judah in a network of unequal political relationships; royal, administrative and biblical evidence.
limits: Not a comprehensive political history of every reign.
Biblical books are literary and theological evidence as well as sources used critically in political reconstruction.
No manuscript or museum photographs reproduced.
A later Elephantine petition (407 BCE) is explicitly outside the atlas’s c. 450 endpoint.

periods.title: A campaign leaves a list, not a border.
periods.north: Northern communities within Egypt’s campaign horizon
periods.political: Shoshenq I commemorated a Levantine campaign at Karnak. He is generally identified with the Shishak of 1 Kings 14. The biblical narrative reports the removal of Jerusalem’s treasures; the Egyptian monument has a different geographical and royal focus.
periods.people: 1 Kings 14:25–28 places the loss in the temple and royal treasury. It says little about village households. A royal list of places cannot supply their voices or tell us exactly what happened at every named site.
periods.limit: Around 925 is a conventional approximation, not a dated eyewitness itinerary. The Karnak evidence does not independently establish every detail of the Jerusalem episode. The arrow marks a regional campaign, not its route or the extent of lasting Egyptian rule.

passages.label: 1 Kings 14:25–28
passages.note: Shishak and Jerusalem’s treasures; a biblical account of the loss.

periods.localNote: Megiddo and Jerusalem orient the region; they do not outline tenth-century kingdoms.
periods.anchor: Approximate campaign horizon; the shaded interval signals uncertainty, not a twenty-year war.

periods.title: An ally against Assyria becomes a tributary.
periods.political: At Qarqar in 853, Ahab appears among the opponents in Shalmaneser III’s account. In 841, Jehu paid the same Assyrian ruler tribute. These are two different reigns and relationships. Meanwhile Mesha’s monument celebrates Moab’s recovery of territory from Israel.
periods.people: Royal monuments foreground rulers and their gods. Tribute means a transfer of valuables, but the Black Obelisk does not tell us how Jehu collected them. The burden on particular households cannot be calculated from its display.
periods.limit: Shalmaneser’s victory language does not establish permanent occupation after Qarqar. Mesha and 2 Kings 3 present different perspectives on conflict; they are not interchangeable transcripts of one battle.

passages.label: 2 Kings 3:4–27
passages.note: Moab’s tribute, rebellion and a disputed campaign outcome.

passages.label: 2 Kings 9–10
passages.note: Jehu’s coup; Kings does not describe his Assyrian tribute.

edges.label: Israel → Qarqar: participation in the 853 coalition

periods.localNote: Dibon locates Mesha’s monument in Moab. Neighbouring states also exercised power over one another.
periods.anchor: 853 and 841 are distinct anchors. Both are shown together to expose the change in relationship.

periods.title: Protection and conquest can come from the same power.
periods.deck: Tiglath-pileser III, Shalmaneser V and Sargon II
periods.north: Israel: territory lost, then kingdom ended
periods.political: Tiglath-pileser III’s campaigns broke up Israel’s territory. Kings describes Ahaz seeking Assyrian help against Israel and Damascus. Samaria then fell under Shalmaneser V; Sargon II also claimed its conquest and reorganized the region. Direct provincial rule replaced Israel’s monarchy.
periods.people: Deportation and resettlement changed communities, but did not empty the countryside. Recent archaeological research investigates continuity and rural reorganization in the Assyrian provinces. Those who stayed and newcomers belong in the story alongside those removed.
periods.limit: The fall is conventionally placed in 722/721, with Sargon’s suppression and reorganization around 720. Scholars debate how to distribute events between the two reigns. Judah’s appeal is not proof that it caused Assyria’s wider expansion.

passages.label: 2 Kings 15:29; 16:5–9
passages.note: Territorial loss (15:29) and Ahaz’s appeal for protection (16:5–9).

passages.label: 2 Kings 17:3–24
passages.note: Tribute, rebellion, conquest and resettlement, followed by theological explanation.

edges.label: Samaria → Gozan region: one deportation destination in 2 Kings 17:6

periods.localNote: Samaria loses its royal function; Jerusalem’s king remains. Dependence is not identical to annexation.
periods.anchor: 734–720 is a sequence; 722/721 is the disputed conventional fall date, not precision to a single day.

claims.text: Tiglath-pileser III’s campaigns broke up Israel’s territory. Kings describes Ahaz seeking Assyrian help against Israel and Damascus. periods.title: Jerusalem survives. Judah pays.
periods.north: Former Israel under Assyrian provincial rule
periods.south: Judah: devastated but its king remains
periods.political: Sennacherib’s account boasts of Hezekiah’s confinement and tribute, without claiming Jerusalem’s capture. Lachish, by contrast, was taken. His text also describes Egyptian and Kushite intervention in the coastal conflict: Judah was part of a regional struggle.
periods.people: The palace reliefs represent Lachish’s captives. Read them alongside the royal account: a city’s survival is not a measure of the safety of people across the kingdom. The reliefs give victims a visible presence within the conqueror’s chosen story.
periods.limit: The campaign is securely anchored in 701, but the accounts explain its outcome differently. Neither an Assyrian boast nor a biblical deliverance story should silently replace the other. See the comparison below.

passages.label: 2 Kings 18:13–19:37
passages.note: Tribute and devastation, followed by the narrative of Jerusalem’s deliverance.

passages.label: Isaiah 10:5–19
passages.note: Assyria interpreted as an instrument that is itself accountable to God.

periods.localNote: Lachish falls; Jerusalem is not reported captured. The local distinction changes what “victory” means.
periods.anchor: 701 is the campaign date. Surviving prisms and palace reliefs commemorate it later.

periods.title: The throne remains. The choice of king does not.
periods.deck: Egypt and Babylon compete for the Levant
periods.north: Samaria beyond the former northern monarchy
periods.political: Kings reports that Necho II removed Jehoahaz and installed Jehoiakim, extracting tribute. Babylon defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605. The Babylonian Chronicle anchors the capture of Jerusalem in 597; Jehoiachin was deported and Zedekiah installed.
periods.people: 2 Kings 23:35 describes Jehoiakim collecting silver and gold from the people to meet Egypt’s demand. In 597, removal of court members and skilled workers affected both those taken and the society they left behind (2 Kings 24:14–16).
periods.limit: Do not combine 597 with the later destruction of Jerusalem. BM 21946 covers 605–594; it cannot by itself document the temple’s burning in 587/586. Biblical regnal numbering and Babylonian conventions also need careful alignment.

passages.label: 2 Kings 23:29–24:17
passages.note: Necho, imposed kingship, tribute, rebellion and the 597 deportation.

passages.label: Jeremiah 46:2
passages.note: Names the Egyptian defeat at Carchemish under Nebuchadnezzar.

edges.label: Babylon → Carchemish: defeat of Egypt in 605

periods.localNote: Jerusalem is captured in 597, but a dependent monarchy continues under Zedekiah.
periods.anchor: 609, 605 and 597 are separate events, not one uninterrupted campaign.

claims.text: Kings reports that Necho II removed Jehoahaz and installed Jehoiakim, extracting tribute. Babylon defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605. The Babylonian Chronicle anchors the capture of Jerusalem in 597; Jehoiachin was deported and Zedekiah installed.

2 Kings 23:35 describes Jehoiakim collecting silver and gold from the people to meet Egypt’s demand. In 597, removal of court members and skilled workers affected both those taken and the society they left behind (2 Kings 24:14–16).

periods.title: A kingdom ends. Its people have different futures.
periods.deck: Judah and Babylonia after the destruction
periods.north: Samaria: the northern kingdom is not restored
periods.political: After Zedekiah’s rebellion, Jerusalem and its temple were destroyed in 587/586. Kings describes deportation, a population left to cultivate the land, and Gedaliah’s appointment at Mizpah. The end of the kingdom did not mean the disappearance of everyone in Judah.
periods.people: In Babylon, an oil ration list names Jehoiachin and his entourage. It establishes a royal presence abroad, not the circumstances of every exile. Jeremiah 29:4–7 imagines building, planting and family life in exile; Psalm 137 voices grief and remembered violence.
periods.limit: 587 and 586 reflect competing alignments of regnal chronologies; the destruction itself is not in doubt. Lachish’s Hebrew ostraca illuminate communication, but an individual sherd’s function and exact relation to the final crisis can be disputed.

passages.label: 2 Kings 25:1–26
passages.note: Destruction, deportation, those left in the land and Gedaliah at Mizpah.

passages.label: Jeremiah 29:4–7; Psalm 137
passages.note: Read counsel for life abroad beside Psalm 137’s lament; these are different literary voices.

periods.localNote: Mizpah marks an administrative focus in the biblical account. The land was not simply empty.
periods.anchor: 587/586 marks the destruction; exile is an extended and varied condition, not a single departure.

claims.text: After Zedekiah’s rebellion, Jerusalem and its temple were destroyed in 587/586. Kings describes deportation, a population left to cultivate the land, and Gedaliah’s appointment at Mizpah. The end of the kingdom did not mean the disappearance of everyone in Judah.

In Babylon, an oil ration list names Jehoiachin and his entourage. It establishes a royal presence abroad, not the circumstances of every exile. Jeremiah 29:4–7 imagines building, planting and family life in exile; Psalm 137 voices grief and remembered violence.

periods.title: Return does not restore the old kingdom.
periods.deck: Cyrus, Darius and the rebuilding of the temple
periods.north: Samaria within the Persian imperial world
periods.south: Yehud: a province, not a Davidic monarchy
periods.political: Cyrus took Babylon in 539. Ezra attributes authorization for return and temple rebuilding to him; its account places completion in Darius’s sixth year, conventionally 515. These are distinct moments. Judah’s renewed temple existed within Persian government.
periods.people: Ezra 3 describes joy and weeping at the new foundation. Haggai 1 links rebuilding to economic hardship, while Ezra 4 records opposition. “Return” involved rebuilding institutions and negotiating relationships; it was not one simultaneous homecoming for all Judeans.
periods.limit: The Cyrus Cylinder presents a Babylonian ruler chosen by Marduk and restoring cults. It does not name Judah or Jerusalem. It provides a comparison for royal restoration language, not an independent copy of Ezra 1. The scale and timing of return remain debated.

passages.label: Ezra 1:1–4; 6:14–15
passages.note: Authorization in Ezra 1; completion dated in Ezra 6:14–15.

passages.label: Haggai 1; Ezra 3–4
passages.note: Economic strain, mixed emotions and contested rebuilding.

passages.label: Isaiah 44:24–45:7
passages.note: Cyrus’s role interpreted in relation to Israel’s God.

edges.label: Babylonia → Jerusalem: return in Ezra (route and numbers uncertain)

periods.localNote: Jerusalem is a temple centre in Persian Yehud. No precise provincial border is asserted here.
periods.anchor: 539 is Babylon’s fall; 538 is the conventional date for Cyrus’s authorization in Ezra; 515 derives from Ezra’s regnal dating.

claims.text: Cyrus took Babylon in 539. Ezra attributes authorization for return and temple rebuilding to him; its account places completion in Darius’s sixth year, conventionally 515. These are distinct moments. Judah’s renewed temple existed within Persian government.

periods.title: The archive continues beyond the homecoming story.
periods.north: Samaria within the wider imperial administration
periods.political: The change from Babylonian to Persian rule did not erase the communities formed through deportation. Legal and administrative records let us ask how people worked, held land and met obligations across that political transition.
periods.people: Alstola’s research finds rural land-for-service arrangements alongside urban occupations and differences in status. These records complicate the idea that every deportee was enslaved in the same way, or that every family left Babylonia when return became possible.
periods.limit: The Yāhūdu material lacks secure excavation provenance; its precise location is uncertain, so it is not pinned to a guessed village. Contract archives overrepresent recorded transactions and cannot reconstruct every household’s beliefs or feelings.

passages.label: Jeremiah 29:4–14
passages.note: A biblical literary perspective on settlement, hope and the duration of exile.

periods.localNote: Yehud and communities in Babylonia coexist. This final window overlaps the exile and return periods.
periods.anchor: A broad documentary horizon, overlapping earlier windows; 572–450 is a teaching window, not the exact limits of every archive.

debates.question: Samaria: whose conquest and when?
positions: Conventional 722/721 fall; Shalmaneser V associated with the siege and conquest.
Sargon II claims conquest; 720 suppression and provincial consolidation are distinguished in recent research.
debates.policy: Display 734–720 as sequence and explain 722/721 uncertainty; do not treat a royal claim as a transparent timestamp.

debates.question: Silver tribute in 701?
debates.policy: Show discrepancy, avoid silently selecting an explanation; gold agrees at 30.

debates.question: Cyrus Cylinder and return?
positions: No direct mention of Jerusalem and no independent reproduction of Ezra’s decree.
debates.policy: Distinguish Babylonian legitimation through Marduk from Ezra’s theological frame.

debates.question: Empty land / universal return?
positions: Biblical narratives themselves name people left in Judah.
Administrative research documents varied, enduring communities in Babylonia.
debates.policy: No total-population claims or guessed migration numbers.

debates.question: What kind of document is Lachish Letter II?
debates.policy: Museum bibliography records the debate; do not quote it as an unquestioned last battlefield dispatch.

geography.borderPolicy: No political polygons. No exact Yāhūdu location. Nile Delta and Gozan labels represent regions. Mizpah / Tell en-Nasbeh identification explicitly labelled conventional.
geography.arrows: Schematic participant/destination relationships, not itineraries. Coalition and 841 tribute coexist only in the explicitly multi-event 853–841 window.

outstandingResearch: Full modern editions of the Assyrian corpus would deepen philological comparison; no claim of full collation is made.
Karnak plates and uncertain toponyms need specialist study before any exact campaign map.
No attempt to estimate total numbers deported or returning from biased surviving samples.
Yehud’s changing provincial limits require dedicated regional research before territorial drawing.
Full archaeological reports and administrative editions remain deeper reading, not silently assimilated evidence.
